justification: run-code is green (19 blocks, 9 executed), run by me from PowerShell. Sources opened this round: Microsoft Learn List<T>.Add (O(1) when Count < Capacity, 'becomes an O(n) operation' - quoted correctly), Capacity ('is increased by automatically reallocating the internal array'; setter O(n) in the new capacity - both as cited), TrimExcess (90 percent rule plus the 'might change in future releases' note, now mentioned), Dictionary.Add ('approaches an O(1) operation' / O(n) on growth), and List.cs on main (DefaultCapacity = 4; GetNewCapacity line identical to the quoted one, Array.MaxLength clamp, raise-to-minimum; EnsureCapacity -> Grow -> GetNewCapacity; setter does new T[value] + Array.Copy(_items, newItems, _size); TrimExcess uses 0.9; the only allocation sites are constructors, the Capacity setter, GrowForInsertion and ToArray, so no removal path shrinks). Cornell lec21 has the 3-unit charge with the same three-way split and Phi = 2n - m, and the article says so inline; the CS 3110 textbook uses the banker/physicist names; CLRS 4th ed. ch. 16 is amortized analysis with multipop and the binary counter. Re-derived: trace total 1020; aggregate n + <2n; bank balances for charge 3 (2,6,6,...; lowest 2) and charge 2 (1,1,-3,-11,...; first debt at #9); Phi = max(0, 2 Count - Capacity) gives <=3 / exactly 3 and differs from the bank by the constant 4; additive n^2/(2k) (499.5 and 124,999.5 check); geometric bound n g/(g-1) now correctly qualified 'ignoring rounding'; breakit arithmetic (4*n^2/2 = 3.2 GB; trim fires after each doubling since n < 0.9*2n, giving 12 bytes * n per append = 9.6 GB); 2n - popcount(n) with popcount(10^6) = 7 and worst increment 20; exercise answers (10/20/40 with 30 copies; charge 1 + g/(g-1) = 4; 2048 copies per thrash round = 20,480,000; 2,097,148 slots = 8.4 MB; quarter-full hysteresis gives at least capacity/4 cheap operations, 4 coins suffice). Figure 1 and Figure 3 coordinates are to scale against the printed data. No factual error found, so no cap applies. Round-1 check: all eight technical minors are genuinely fixed (rounding caveat, hysteresis constant and coin argument, average-case vs expected wording for Dictionary, section renamed and exercises moved mid-article, multipop sentence, 'nine calls' sentence, 'everybody' claim removed, TrimExcess 'currently' + page-mapping clause). The adsense/design majors are also addressed in the source: diagrams are now 360-wide with annotations under the drawing, the four-column table became a list, a third figure was added, the last section is no longer 'Exercises', and docs/crosslinks/complexity/amortized-analysis.md exists with six sensible links and clear sibling boundaries. Against the ranking pages: yourbasic is a 400-word aggregate-only proof on a toy array; Wikipedia lists the three methods with a dynamic array and queue but no measurements, no growth-factor analysis and no failure modes; the Cornell lecture/textbook match this article on rigor but have no running code, no real-library evidence, no latency measurement, no spec-vs-implementation discipline and no 'how the guarantee is lost' section. The article is at least as rigorous as the best of them and clearly ahead on evidence and practical caveats. What remains are nits.

issues.location: Exercise 'Find the bug in the shrink rule', solution: 'The standard fix is hysteresis: halve only when the array is a quarter full.'
issues.problem: 'The standard fix' is asserted without a source, although the article cites CLRS chapter 16 elsewhere and that chapter's dynamic-table section is exactly where the halve-at-one-quarter rule comes from. The brief asks for the citation where the claim is made.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add an inline attribution, e.g. '(the rule analysed in the dynamic-tables section of CLRS chapter 16)'.

issues.location: 'Add up the whole sequence', cost-model paragraph ('the runtime zero-fills the new array') and the latency paragraph ('which the operating system has to map in as it is first touched')
issues.problem: Two true but unsourced mechanism claims stated as fact. The Capacity doc citation that follows supports O(n) in the new capacity, not the zero-filling; the page-mapping clause has no source at all and the experiment does not separate it from the copy.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite the C# language reference on array elements being default-initialized, or soften to 'a new array starts zeroed, which costs time proportional to its length'; phrase the page-mapping clause as a likely contributor ('fresh memory the operating system typically maps on first touch') rather than a measured fact.

issues.location: Figure 1, staircase path starting 'M40 311.25' and the shaded polygon
issues.problem: The drawing shows Capacity 4 at Count 0, while the trace directly above it prints 'Empty list: Capacity 0' and the first growth at Add #1. Steps are also drawn at Count 4, 8, ... although the growth happens on the following Add. At this scale the second point is invisible, but the first contradicts the page's own output.
issues.fixLooksLike: Start the staircase at the origin with a vertical rise to 4 at the first Add (or say in the caption that the empty list's capacity of 0 is omitted).

issues.location: 'Amortized is not average-case', Dictionary paragraph: 'provided the table grows geometrically'
issues.problem: The reader is left not knowing whether Dictionary<TKey,TValue> actually does. The article is otherwise careful to check implementation claims against source; here it hedges without checking.
issues.fixLooksLike: One clause with a citation to Dictionary.cs (current .NET resizes to a prime at least twice the old size), marked as an implementation detail, or an explicit 'this page does not verify Dictionary's growth policy; the hash-tables article does'.

issues.location: 'Amortized is not average-case', line ending 'costs more than 3*n*. ' and bullet 'Worst-case ... its only fault is that it can be pessimistic'
issues.problem: Trailing whitespace after '3n.'; 'no adversary can pick a sequence ... more than 3n' silently relies on the cost model and the empty default-constructed list defined three sections earlier; 'its only fault' is an unneeded absolute.
issues.fixLooksLike: Trim the whitespace; write 'more than 3n under the cost model above'; 'its drawback is that it can be pessimistic'.
